title: Do Activity-Based Incentive Plans Work? Evidence from a Large-Scale Field Intervention
abstract: Many firms incorporate activity-based incentive (ABI) compensation into their pay plans. These ABIs are based on salespeople’s activity measures derived from their call reports. Despite their prevalence and theory-based expectations, there is a distinct lack of empirical work studying the sales productivity effects of ABI pay. With the cooperation of a large pharmaceutical firm, the authors conducted a three-year-long intervention based on a “treatment-removal” design. Their first intervention added modest ABI pay for frontline salespeople and their supervisors across 305 sales territories; the second intervention removed ABI pay from the salespeople; and the third intervention removed ABI pay from the supervisors as well, returning to the status quo. Using detailed territory-level data from the intervention in conjunction with syndicated market-level data and employing synthetic control procedures, the authors find sales gains of around 6%–9% from each of the two ABI interventions relative to the no-ABI baseline. These effects are moderated by the number of salespeople in a territory, with territories with more salespeople showing larger effects. Analyses of activity effects show that when supervisors are paid ABIs, they exert behavior control downward on salespeople. Managerially, both ABI schemes improve performance over an output-only pay plan. Between the two, a rudimentary gross profit impact calculation shows that ABIs targeted at supervisors alone are more efficient than ABIs targeted at both salespeople and their supervisors. The results support tying compensation to call reports despite the potential for self-serving biases in these measures because supervisors are able to exercise more behavior control with ABIs.

summary.oneLiner: In a pharma field experiment, activity-based incentives raised sales 6–9% over output-only pay, with supervisor-only ABIs proving more efficient.
summary.overview: Many firms pay salespeople partly on activity measures, such as the calls logged in their call reports, rather than only on sales. This study ran a three-year intervention with a large pharmaceutical firm across 305 sales territories, adding activity-based incentives (ABIs) for salespeople and supervisors, then removing them in stages. Using a synthetic control method (a statistical comparison built from similar units that did not receive the treatment), the authors estimate sales gains of about 6–9% from each ABI scheme relative to no ABI pay. Supervisor-paid ABIs were the more efficient option in a rudimentary gross profit calculation, and the authors argue this supports tying pay to call reports despite possible self-serving reporting.
summary.question: Do activity-based incentive pay plans improve the sales productivity of frontline salespeople, and how do they compare with output-only pay plans?
summary.method: A three-year field intervention using a treatment-removal design: ABI pay was added, then removed from salespeople, then removed from supervisors as well. Synthetic control procedures were used, combined with syndicated market-level data, to compare outcomes against a no-ABI baseline.
summary.data: Detailed territory-level data from a large pharmaceutical firm covering 305 sales territories over the three-year intervention, combined with syndicated market-level data.
findings: Each of the two ABI interventions produced sales gains of around 6%–9% relative to the no-ABI baseline.
The sales effects are moderated by the number of salespeople in a territory, with territories that have more salespeople showing larger effects.
When supervisors are paid ABIs, they exert behavior control downward on salespeople.
Both ABI schemes improve performance over an output-only pay plan.
A rudimentary gross profit calculation suggests ABIs targeted at supervisors alone are more efficient than ABIs targeted at both salespeople and supervisors.
The authors state the results support tying compensation to call reports despite potential self-serving biases in these measures, because supervisors can exercise more behavior control with ABIs.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors state that, for managers, both ABI schemes outperform output-only pay, and that paying supervisors alone may be the more efficient design. They argue that tying compensation to call reports can be justified despite self-serving biases, because supervisors gain more behavior control through ABIs.
